t: Peter, the fisherman named the Rock
p: The letter opens with the apostle's Greek nickname, not his birth name, Simon.
b: The writer calls himself Petros, the Greek form of the Aramaic nickname Kephas, 'Rock', that Jesus gave Simon (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42). He adds no other title than 'an apostle of Jesus Christ'. Later he calls himself 'your fellow elder' (5:1). Whether Peter himself wrote the letter, wrote it through a helper, or whether a group in Rome wrote it in his name after his death is discussed in the opening pages (Authorship). The Plain follows the text as written.

p: Two words set the tone of the whole letter: God's choice, and life as outsiders.
b: Eklektois parepidemois joins two ideas. Eklektos, 'chosen', is Israel's word for itself (Deuteronomy 7:6; Isaiah 43:20), which 2:9 quotes. Parepidemos is a person staying for a time in a place that is not home; Abraham uses the word of himself in the Greek of Genesis 23:4. The site keeps 'temporary residents' for parepidemoi and 'resident aliens' for paroikoi (2:11). The words return at 1:17 and 2:11 and frame the letter. Whether they describe the readers' legal and social standing or their spiritual state as people whose home is with God is debated: see the note at 2:11.

p: The Jewish word for Jews living outside the land of Israel. Were the readers Jewish believers, Gentiles, or both?
b: Diaspora, 'scattering', was the Greek-speaking Jews' word for their communities outside the land (John 7:35: 'the Dispersion in the Greek world'; compare James 1:1). Readers have taken it three ways. (1) Jewish believers. Eusebius, following Origen, says Peter 'preached in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and Asia to the Jews of the dispersion' (Church History 3.1.2), and Calvin held that 'dispersion' 'can apply only to the Jews', since Peter was the apostle to the circumcised (Galatians 2:7-8). (2) Mixed churches. Calvin's translator John Owen replied in a note that nothing proves the letter was 'written only to believing Jews', and that 4:3 'seems clearly to shew that Peter included the believing Gentiles'. (3) Mostly Gentiles. Many modern interpreters, the NET Bible's notes among them, take 'Dispersion' as a picture applied to Gentile Christians: they lived in 'the futile way of life that your fathers passed on to you' (1:18) and once did 'what the Gentiles want' (4:3). On this reading, Peter gives a church of former pagans Israel's names (2:9-10) without ever mentioning Israel or the Jews.

a: Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia
p: The list covers most of what is now Turkey north of the Taurus Mountains.
b: All five were Roman provincial names in the first century; Pontus and Bithynia formed one province. They take in the whole of Asia Minor north and west of the Taurus range, a vast area with cities, farms and villages. One proposal is that the order, starting at Pontus on the Black Sea and ending at Bithynia next to it, is the route a courier would ride in a loop. Pontus, Cappadocia and Asia are named among the crowd at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), and Paul was kept from preaching in Asia and Bithynia (Acts 16:6-7).

a: what God the Father knew beforehand
p: Greek prognosis: God's knowing ahead of time, the word later debates about election turn on.
b: Kata prognosin theou patros, 'according to the foreknowledge of God the Father', is most naturally joined to 'chosen' in 1:1. The same family of words is used of Christ in 1:20 ('known in advance') and in Acts 2:23 ('what God knew ahead of time') and Romans 8:29. Readers differ on what the knowing means: that God chose on the basis of what he knew people would do, or that his 'knowing' is itself a loving decision to make them his own, as 'know' often means in the Old Testament (Amos 3:2). See the topic Election and the cards at Romans 8:29 and Ephesians 1:4. The verse itself names the Father, the Spirit and Jesus Christ together, a pattern later read as one of the roots of the doctrine of the Trinity.

a: set apart as holy by the Spirit
p: Hagiasmos is the act of making holy; the theme returns in 1:15-16.
b: En hagiasmo pneumatos could be 'by the Spirit's sanctifying' (the Spirit does it) or 'in holiness of spirit' (the readers' own spirit). Most readers take the first, because the verse names the Father and Jesus Christ beside it. The Plain gives that reading. 'Holy' is the letter's key word for what God's choice makes of people (1:15-16; 2:5, 9).

a: sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ
t: Sprinkled with blood: the covenant at Sinai
p: Obedience and sprinkled blood together recall the day Israel promised to obey and Moses splashed the blood.
b: At Sinai the people said they would obey all the LORD had spoken, and Moses then threw the blood of the offerings on them, calling it 'the blood of the covenant' (Exodus 24:7-8). Peter joins the same two things, obedience and sprinkled blood, with the blood now Christ's. Hebrews 9:18-22 and 12:24 use the same picture. Some readers also hear the sprinkling that cleansed priests and the unclean (Leviticus 8:30; Numbers 19).

p: 'Grace and peace be multiplied' is a greeting found in Jewish letters in Daniel's Greek and later.
b: The verb plethyntheie, 'may it be multiplied', appears in the greeting of 2 Peter 1:2 and Jude 1:2 as well. Paul's letters say 'Grace to you and peace' without it (Romans 1:7). On this site Jude 1:2 reads 'Mercy to you, and peace, and love: may they be multiplied', and the Plain here follows that wording.

a: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
t: A Jewish blessing turned to Christ
p: The opening copies the Jewish prayer form 'Blessed be God, who ...', as Paul does.
b: Jewish prayer often begins 'Blessed are you, LORD', and then names what God has done (compare Psalm 41:13; Genesis 24:27). Peter's opening line is the same in Greek as 2 Corinthians 1:3 and Ephesians 1:3, and the Plain matches 2 Corinthians 1:3 word for word. The God of Israel is now named as 'the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ', and the deed he is blessed for is the resurrection.

p: Anagennao, 'beget again', appears only here and in 1:23 in the New Testament.
b: The verb is used only twice in the Bible, here and in 1:23. John speaks of being 'born from above' (John 3:3) and Titus of 'the bath of new birth' (Titus 3:5), with other words. In 1 Peter the new birth comes through Christ's resurrection (1:3) and through 'God's word, which is alive and remains' (1:23), and it makes the readers newborn babies who need milk (2:2). The image may have been especially strong for people who had cut ties with their own families' gods (1:18).

a: cannot decay, cannot be stained and cannot wither
p: In Greek the three adjectives sound alike: aphtharton, amianton, amaranton.
b: Each word begins with the Greek 'not' (a-). Aphthartos is what does not rot; amiantos what is not stained; amarantos what does not wither, the word from which the amaranth flower took its name. The inheritance of the land of Israel could be defiled (Jeremiah 2:7; Numbers 35:34) and lost; this one cannot. The same family of words returns: the 'seed that cannot decay' (1:23), the 'wreath of glory that never withers' (5:4).
orig: ἄφθαρτον καὶ ἀμίαντον καὶ ἀμάραντον (aphtharton kai amianton kai amaranton)

p: Israel's inheritance was the land; here it is kept in heaven.
b: Kleronomia is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's share of the promised land (Numbers 26:53-56; Joshua 11:23). For readers called 'temporary residents' who had no land to inherit, Peter places the inheritance in the heavens, where nothing can take it. 3:9 and 3:7 ('co-heirs') return to it.

p: Phroureo is what soldiers do when they hold a town.
b: The verb is used of a garrison guarding a city (2 Corinthians 11:32). God's power is pictured as a guard posted around the readers, 'through faith', until the end. Philippians 4:7 uses the same verb of God's peace guarding hearts.

a: Over this you shout for joy
t: Joy now, or joy to come?
p: The Greek can be read as 'you rejoice' or as a command, and the time of the joy is debated.
b: Agalliasthe can be indicative ('you shout for joy') or imperative ('shout for joy!'); most take it as a statement. Some read it as a present with a future sense: you will rejoice at the last time (1:5). 'Over this' (en ho) may point back to the whole hope just described, or to 'the last time'. The same verb returns in 1:8 and 4:13, always with suffering close by.

p: The letter's sufferings are mostly slander, insults and pressure from neighbors and households.
b: The trials the letter describes are being slandered as wrongdoers (2:12; 3:16), insulted for the name of Christ (4:14), mocked for leaving old habits (4:4), and, for slaves and wives, suffering in households headed by unbelievers (2:18-20; 3:1-6). Many scholars read this as local hostility, not an empire-wide persecution by law; others connect it with the trials of Christians that Pliny describes in Bithynia-Pontus around AD 112. See the opening pages (Setting).

a: which perishes even though fire tests it
p: The refiner's fire is an old picture of God testing his people.
b: Gold was heated to burn off what was mixed into it. Proverbs 17:3 and Malachi 3:2-3 picture God as a refiner of hearts and of the priests, and Zechariah 13:9 speaks of refining a people 'like silver' and testing them 'like gold'. Peter adds a twist: even refined gold still perishes in the end, but tested faith lasts. The image comes back in the 'fiery ordeal' of 4:12.

p: Apokalypsis, 'uncovering', is the word behind 'revelation'.
b: Peter uses apokalypsis for Christ's return (1:7, 13; 4:13) and the verb for the salvation and glory to be revealed (1:5; 5:1). The Plain says 'unveiled' to keep the picture of something now hidden being uncovered. The same noun gives the book of Revelation its name (Revelation 1:1).
orig: ἐν ἀποκαλύψει Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (en apokalypsei Iesou Christou)

a: You love him without having seen him
t: Loving one they have not seen
p: Polycarp of Smyrna echoed this verse early in the 100s.
b: The readers, unlike the writer (5:1), had never seen Jesus. Compare 'Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed' (John 20:29). Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians (chapter 1), written early in the 100s, uses this verse: 'In whom, though now you see Him not, you believe, and believing, rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory' (as New Advent's translation renders it). It is one of the earliest signs that 1 Peter was known and read.

p: Psyche in the Bible usually means the whole living person, not a part of one.
b: Psyche stands for the Hebrew nefesh, the living self. 'Salvation for your souls' means salvation for you, not for an inner part rescued from the body: the hope is a resurrection (1:3). Peter uses the word again for 'eight souls' in the ark (3:20), where it simply means eight people, and in 4:19.

a: which time, or what sort of time
p: The Greek tina e poion kairon may mean 'which person or what time'.
b: Tina may go with kairon, 'which time or what sort of time', or stand alone: 'whom, or what time'. On the second reading the prophets wanted to know who the Messiah would be and when he would come. Both fit the grammar. The Plain takes the first, the more common choice, because tina and poion both seem to describe the same noun; the other is a real possibility.
orig: εἰς τίνα ἢ ποῖον καιρὸν (eis tina e poion kairon)

a: the Spirit of Christ within them
t: The Spirit of Christ in the prophets
p: Peter says the Spirit that spoke in Israel's prophets was 'the Spirit of Christ'.
b: Readers have understood this in several ways: the pre-existent Christ himself spoke through the prophets by his Spirit (a common view among the church fathers, and one Augustine uses for 3:19); the Spirit that spoke of Christ, that is, the prophetic Spirit pointing to the Messiah; or the same Holy Spirit later given by Christ (1:12). 2 Peter 1:21 says the prophets 'spoke from God' as the Holy Spirit carried them. Jewish readers have always read the prophets as speaking to their own times and to Israel's future, without reference to Jesus.

a: the sufferings that would come to Christ and the glories after them
p: The pattern of the whole letter in one phrase.
b: Luke 24:26 has Jesus ask whether the Messiah did not have to suffer and then enter his glory. Peter makes the same pattern the shape of his letter: Christ's suffering and glory (1:11; 3:18-22), the readers' suffering and glory (4:13; 5:1, 10). The prophets most often read this way are Isaiah 52:13-53:12 (quoted in 2:22-25) and Psalm 22.

a: Angels would love to bend down and peer into them
p: Parakypto is to stoop and look, as the disciples looked into the empty tomb.
b: The same verb is used of Peter and the beloved disciple bending down to look into Jesus' tomb (Luke 24:12; John 20:5, 11). Angels, who serve God in heaven, do not have what the readers have been told; they long to look into it.

a: tuck up the robes of your mind
p: The Greek says 'gird up the loins of your mind', an image from long robes.
b: People wore long robes and tucked them into a belt to run or work (Exodus 12:11, where Israel eats the Passover with belts fastened; Luke 12:35). Peter applies the picture to the mind: get it ready for action. The KJV keeps 'gird up the loins of your mind'; the Plain keeps the robe and says what it means.
orig: ἀναζωσάμενοι τὰς ὀσφύας τῆς διανοίας (anazosamenoi tas osphyas tes dianoias)

p: Nepho is literally 'be sober' and means a clear head, ready to act.
b: Peter uses the verb three times (1:13; 4:7; 5:8). It is more than not being drunk: it is the alertness of a guard on watch, the same verb Paul uses in 1 Thessalonians 5:6. On this site the second and third uses read 'keep a clear head'.

a: Do not shape yourselves to fit
t: Do not be shaped to fit
p: The verb is Romans 12:2's 'Stop shaping yourselves to fit this age'.
b: Syschematizomai occurs only here and in Romans 12:2. The Plain uses the same English. What the readers are not to be shaped by is 'the desires you had before, when you did not know': the time before they knew God. That phrase fits Gentile converts, who had not known Israel's God (compare Acts 17:30; Galatians 4:8).

a: You will be holy, because I am holy
p: Quoted from Leviticus, where it sets Israel apart from the nations.
b: The words come from Leviticus 19:2 (also 11:44-45; 20:7), in the section often called the Holiness Code. The site's Leviticus 19:2 has 'You will be holy, because I am holy' from the Hebrew; the Greek here matches the Septuagint, and the English is the same. In Leviticus, holiness meant living by laws that marked Israel off from the nations around it, in food, worship, family and the treatment of the poor. Peter gives the call to Gentile believers, without the food laws, as a call to live differently among the nations (2:12).

p: Aprosopolemptos: literally 'not taking hold of faces', a Hebrew idiom for bias.
b: The word is built from the Hebrew idiom 'lift up the face' of someone, that is, show them favor. God judges each person's 'work' (singular: the whole of a life) with no regard for rank. Acts 10:34 and Romans 2:11 use related words, and Colossians 3:25 says 'There is no favoritism.' For slaves and wives in hard households (2:18-3:6), a judge who does not take sides with the powerful mattered.

a: during your time as resident aliens
p: Paroikia is the time a foreigner spends living in a land not his own.
b: Acts 13:17 uses it of Israel's stay in Egypt. Peter calls the readers' whole life now a paroikia: they live among others whose home this is, and their own home lies ahead. See the note at 2:11 on the social and the spiritual readings.

p: Lytroo is the word for buying back a slave or captive.
b: The verb and its noun are used for the price paid to set a slave or prisoner free, and for God's 'redeeming' Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). Jesus speaks of giving 'his life as a ransom in place of many' (Mark 10:45), and Titus 2:14 says 'so that he could redeem us out of every kind of lawlessness'. Here the readers are ransomed not from Egypt but from the 'futile way of life that your fathers passed on to you'.

a: the futile way of life that your fathers passed on to you
p: A Jew would hardly call the ancestral way of life 'futile'; this points to Gentile readers.
b: Patroparadotos, 'handed down from the fathers', was a word of honor in the Greek world: one kept the ancestral customs and gods. Jews spoke of their own ancestral traditions with pride (Galatians 1:14). That Peter calls the readers' inherited way of life mataios, 'futile', a word the Greek Old Testament uses for idols (Leviticus 17:7; Jeremiah 8:19), is one of the main reasons many scholars think the readers were mostly Gentiles. Turning away from the family gods also explains why their neighbors and families resented them (4:3-4).

a: like that of a lamb with no flaw and no stain
p: The Passover lamb and the offerings had to be without defect.
b: The Passover lamb was to be 'a sound and whole animal' (Exodus 12:5), and so were the animals offered at the altar (Leviticus 22:19-25). The word 'ransomed' just before (1:18) recalls the rescue from Egypt, so most readers hear the Passover here. Isaiah 53:7 compares the servant to a lamb led to slaughter, and John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God' (John 1:29).

t: Known before the foundation of the world
p: Christ was 'known in advance' before creation, and appeared 'in the last of the times'.
b: Proegnosmenou uses the same word family as the 'foreknowledge' of 1:2. Many read it to mean that God planned the rescue through Christ before he made the world (compare Revelation 13:8; Ephesians 1:4). Others take it as teaching Christ's existence before his birth, since what is 'brought into the open' must already have been there. The phrase 'the last of the times' places the readers in the final age (compare 4:7; Hebrews 1:2).

a: a love of the brothers that does not pretend
p: Philadelphia is family love, the love of brothers and sisters, for fellow believers.
b: In ordinary Greek philadelphia was the love between siblings. Christians used it for one another (Romans 12:10; 1 Thessalonians 4:9; Hebrews 13:1). Peter uses the brother words often: 'Love the brothers' (2:17), 'love like brothers' (3:8), 'your brothers in the world' (5:9). The Greek masculine plural includes women; this site keeps 'brothers' with the gloss 'brothers and sisters', as in Romans and Acts. A church made of people whose own families might reject them (4:4) became their family.

p: Ektenos: 'stretched out', with effort, without letting up.
b: The adverb pictures something pulled tight or stretched to its full length. It is used of earnest prayer (Acts 12:5, the church praying for Peter in prison) and returns in 4:8, where the adjective describes love 'that never slackens'. The Plain uses the same word in both places so the link shows.

a: God's word, which is alive and remains
t: Which is alive and remains: the word, or God?
p: The Greek can say that the word lives and remains, or that God does.
b: Dia logou zontos theou kai menontos can be read 'through the living and remaining word of God' or 'through the word of the God who lives and remains' (compare Daniel 6:26, where God is 'the living God' who 'endures'). The quotation that follows, 'the Lord's word remains forever' (1:25), favors the first, and the Plain follows it. On 'remains' (meno), the site's word for this verb, see the note at 1:25.
orig: διὰ λόγου ζῶντος θεοῦ καὶ μένοντος (dia logou zontos theou kai menontos)

t: Isaiah 40: the grass and the word
p: Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 in its Greek form, which differs from the Hebrew in two places.
b: The site's Isaiah 40:6, from the Hebrew, reads 'All flesh is grass, / and all its loyal love is like a wildflower', and 40:8 ends 'but our God's word will stand forever'. The Greek that Peter quotes has 'glory' for the Hebrew hesed, 'loyal love', and 'the Lord's word' for 'our God's word'. Isaiah's words open the message of comfort to the exiles in Babylon, which fits a letter to 'the Dispersion' sent from 'Babylon' (5:13).

p: Meno, 'remain, stay', is the same verb in 1:23 and in Isaiah's line.
b: The Plain uses 'remains' for meno both in 1:23 and here, so the reader can see that Peter's phrase about the word 'which is alive and remains' was taken from the Isaiah quotation. The site's word for this verb is 'remain' (as John 15:4-5).
orig: μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (menei eis ton aiona)

a: brought to you as good news
p: Euangelizo, 'announce good news', the root of 'gospel' and 'evangelize'.
b: Isaiah 40:9 itself calls on a 'bearer of good news' to announce God's coming, and the Greek uses this verb there. Peter says that the lasting 'word' of Isaiah is the same word that was announced to his readers as good news (compare 1:12; 4:6, 17).

p: Apotithemi is the word for taking off clothes.
b: The same verb is used of taking off the old self (Ephesians 4:22, 25) and laying aside every weight (Hebrews 12:1; James 1:21). Many scholars think it belongs to the language of baptism, when converts took off their old clothes and put on new ones.

p: Logikon gala may mean 'milk of the word', 'spiritual milk' or 'milk for the mind'.
b: Logikos is built on logos, 'word' or 'reason'. In Romans 12:1 the site renders it 'sensible worship'. Here many read 'the milk of the word', because Peter has just spoken of the word that gives new birth (1:23-25); the KJV has 'the sincere milk of the word'. Others take it as 'spiritual' (not literal) milk, or as nourishment for the reasoning mind. The Plain gives the word reading, which keeps the link with 1:23-25.
orig: τὸ λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα (to logikon adolon gala)

p: Adolos, 'without trickery', answers the 'trickery' (dolos) of 2:1.
b: Merchants used adolos for goods that were pure, with nothing mixed in: grain, oil, milk. Peter has just told the readers to take off all dolos, 'trickery' (2:1). The milk they are to crave is a-dolos, with no trickery in it. The Plain keeps the word play.

p: Peter borrows Psalm 34:8, the psalm he quotes again in 3:10-12.
b: Psalm 34:8 reads 'Taste and see: the LORD is good!' The Greek of the psalm has chrestos, 'kind, good', and Peter takes it over. In Greek chrestos sounded almost like Christos, and some readers think the play was meant. For Peter 'the Lord' is Christ, the living stone of 2:4.

p: Stones are dead things; this one lives, and makes the stones built on it live.
b: Peter joins a string of Scripture texts about a stone (2:6-8) to the picture of a temple. Christ is the stone 'that is alive' because he was raised (1:3). People 'threw him out as worthless', the verb of Psalm 118:22 ('A stone that the builders threw out'), which Jesus applied to himself (Matthew 21:42) and which Peter quotes before the council in Acts 4:11.

t: A spiritual house: a temple made of people
p: Oikos pneumatikos: 'house' is a common word for the temple.
b: In the Greek Old Testament the temple is often 'the house of the Lord'. Here the readers are the stones and Christ the cornerstone. Paul calls the church God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21-22). Peter's word 'spiritual' may mean 'made by the Spirit', or 'not made of stone'. Some read 'house' as 'household', as in 4:17 ('God's house'), which joins the temple and family images.

p: The whole community is called a priesthood that offers sacrifices: what that means is a dividing question.
b: Hierateuma, 'priesthood', is a collective noun: the body of priests, not each individual. The 'spiritual sacrifices' are not named here, but the New Testament elsewhere speaks of offering one's body (Romans 12:1), praise and doing good (Hebrews 13:15-16), and gifts to those in need (Philippians 4:18). How this common priesthood relates to ordained ministers is one of the deepest divisions between the churches: see the card 'Where Christians differ' on this chapter.

a: Look, I am setting in Zion a stone
p: Peter quotes Isaiah 28:16 as Romans 9:33 does, close to the Greek of Isaiah.
b: The site's Isaiah 28:16, from the Hebrew, says 'Look, I have laid a stone in Zion for a foundation, / a stone that has been tested, / a cornerstone of great worth' and ends 'Whoever believes will not hurry.' The Greek of Isaiah has 'will not be put to shame', and so do Peter and Paul. Romans 9:33 joins this verse to Isaiah 8:14, as Peter does in 2:8, and the site's Romans reads 'the one who believes in him will not be put to shame'. Because both apostles join the same verses in nearly the same Greek, many scholars think they drew on a collection of stone texts already used in the church.

p: Akrogoniaios is the stone at the corner of the foundation; some read it as the top stone.
b: The word comes from Isaiah 28:16 in the Greek, where the stone is laid 'in the foundations'. Ephesians 2:20 uses it too: 'with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone'. Some scholars take it as the capstone over an arch or at the top of a wall, and Psalm 118:22's 'head of the corner' (2:7) could point that way. The Plain keeps 'cornerstone', the word of this site's Isaiah 28:16 and Ephesians 2:20.

p: He time may mean 'the honor' or 'the preciousness'.
b: The phrase hymin oun he time tois pisteuousin has no verb: 'to you, then, the honor (or preciousness), you who believe'. It picks up entimon, 'of great worth', in 2:6. It can mean 'to you who believe, he is precious' (the KJV) or 'the honor is yours, you who believe', answering the promise that the believer 'will not be put to shame' (2:6). The Plain takes the second, because the sentence sets the believers' honor against the unbelievers' stumbling; the KJV's reading is the main alternative.

a: a stone that makes people stumble and a rock that makes them fall
p: Peter and Paul quote the same Greek words, which are closer to the Hebrew than to the Septuagint.
b: The site's Isaiah 8:14 says the LORD 'will become a holy place, / and a stone that people strike their foot on, / and a rock they trip over'. Peter's wording, the same as Romans 9:33 ('a stone that makes people stumble and a rock that makes them fall'), is close to the Hebrew. The Greek of Isaiah 8:14 in Swete's edition says almost the reverse, that the people will meet him 'not as a stumbling stone'. In Isaiah the stone is the LORD himself; Peter and Paul apply it to Christ.

a: that is what they were also set for
p: Eis ho kai etethesan: 'to which they were also appointed'. The question is: appointed to what?
b: The verb tithemi is the one God uses in 2:6, 'I am setting in Zion a stone'. God sets the stone, and the unbelieving were 'set' for stumbling. Some read this as God's decree that certain people would disbelieve. Others say what was appointed is the outcome: those who refuse to obey will stumble, as a rule God has fixed, without God deciding who will refuse. Others again stress that the same people can still come to faith (2:12 hopes outsiders will 'give glory to God'). See the topic Election.
orig: εἰς ὃ καὶ ἐτέθησαν (eis ho kai etethesan)

t: Exodus 19:6: Israel's titles given to the church
p: Peter takes the titles God gave Israel at Sinai and gives them to his readers.
b: At Sinai God told Israel 'you will be for me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6). The Greek of Exodus has basileion hierateuma, 'a royal priesthood', and Peter uses it word for word. 'A chosen family' and 'a people God has made his own ... to tell out the mighty acts' come from the Greek of Isaiah 43:20-21 ('my people, my chosen one', 'This people I shaped for myself. / They will recount my praise'). Revelation 1:6 and 5:10 say the same of believers ('a kingdom, priests'). How this relates to Israel, which Peter never names, is a question for the J lens and the topic church-israel.

p: Aretai usually means 'virtues', but in the Greek Old Testament it can mean praises or great deeds.
b: Isaiah 43:21 in the Greek says God formed his people 'to recount my aretai'; the site's Hebrew-based Isaiah has 'They will recount my praise.' The KJV has 'shew forth the praises'. The Plain says 'mighty acts' because what is told out is what God has done: calling people out of darkness.

p: Peter uses Hosea's names Lo-ammi and Lo-ruhamah, 'Not My People' and 'Not Shown Compassion'.
b: Hosea named his children 'Lo-ruhamah' and 'Lo-ammi' as signs against Israel (Hosea 1:6, 9), and then promised a reversal: 'I will have compassion on Lo-ruhamah, / and I will say to Lo-ammi, "You are my people"' (Hosea 2:23). Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel. Peter, like Paul in Romans 9:25-26, applies the promise to people who had never been God's people. The Greek verb is 'show mercy'; the Plain says 'shown compassion' so the link with Hosea's names stays visible.

a: as resident aliens and temporary residents
t: Resident aliens: social fact or spiritual picture?
p: Were the readers literal outsiders in their towns, or is this a picture of every Christian life?
b: Paroikoi were free foreigners living in a city without citizens' rights; parepidemoi were visitors staying for a while. John H. Elliott's A Home for the Homeless (1981) argued that the readers were resident aliens in a social sense, in conflict with society, and that the letter offers them a home in 'God's house' (2:5; 4:17), as Moses Chin's survey summarizes it. Chin and others reply that the words had long been used in a spiritual sense of life on earth as a stay away from home (Psalm 39:12: 'For I am a foreigner with you, / a lodger, as all my fathers were'). The Greek of that psalm uses both of Peter's words, and so does Abraham in the Greek of Genesis 23:4. Many readers hold that both are true: converts lost standing when they became Christians.

p: Peter speaks of the outsiders as 'the Gentiles', as if his mostly Gentile readers were Israel.
b: The readers had once done 'what the Gentiles want' (4:3), yet now Peter calls their unbelieving neighbors 'the Gentiles'. He writes as a Jew would of Israel among the nations. This is part of how the letter gives the church Israel's place (1:1; 2:9-10). Readers differ on what it means for the Jewish people: that the church has replaced Israel, that Gentile believers have been joined to Israel, or that Peter is using Israel's language as a model without saying anything about Israel itself. See the topic church-israel.

p: Hemera episkopes: the day God comes to look into things, for rescue or for judgment.
b: In the Greek Old Testament God's 'visitation' can be for judgment (Isaiah 10:3) or rescue (Genesis 50:24). Jesus wept over Jerusalem because 'you did not recognize the season when you were visited' (Luke 19:44). Here it may be the day of judgment, when even opponents will admit God's ways, or a day when they themselves are 'visited' and come to faith. Jesus' saying 'so that they see the good you do and give glory to your Father who is in heaven' (Matthew 5:16) lies close behind the verse.

p: Pase anthropine ktisei: literally 'every human creation'.
b: Ktisis normally means 'creation' or 'creature'. Here it is used of human institutions or officials, as the list of the king and governors shows. Some read 'every human creature', submit to every person; but the examples point to authorities. The call is grounded 'because of the Lord', not in fear of punishment. Compare Romans 13:1-7 and Titus 3:1: 'Remind them to submit to rulers and authorities and obey them'.

p: Greek-speaking subjects called the Roman emperor basileus, 'king'.
b: Romans avoided the title 'king' for their emperor, but in the Greek East he was commonly called basileus. The emperor at the time was Nero if the letter is from Peter's lifetime, or, if it is later, one of the emperors from Vespasian to Trajan. The 'governors' (2:14) were the provincial governors of the five regions. Peter tells the readers to 'give honor to the king' (2:17) but to fear God alone. Around AD 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia-Pontus, had people accused as Christians offer 'prayer with incense and wine to your image', the emperor's, something he had heard 'those who are really Christians' cannot be forced to do. See the topic Ruler Worship and the Imperial Cult.

t: Sent by him: the king or God?
p: Di' autou, 'through him', could mean the emperor or the Lord.
b: Grammatically 'him' most naturally means the king of 2:13, who appointed provincial governors. Some read it as God (compare Romans 13:4, where the authority is 'God's servant'). Either way the governors' task is described as it should be: to punish wrongdoers and commend those who do good. Peter does not say what to do when a governor does the opposite, and the readers were already suffering unjustly (2:19-20).

p: Phimoo is to put a muzzle on an animal, and then to silence someone.
b: The same verb is used of muzzling the ox (1 Corinthians 9:9; 1 Timothy 5:18) and of Jesus silencing the Sadducees (Matthew 22:34). The readers' good deeds are to shut the mouths of people who slander them out of ignorance.

p: Theou douloi: the site renders doulos 'slave', even when the master is God.
b: Greek and Roman slavery was a legal state in which a person belonged to another. Many English Bibles say 'servants' when the master is God, but the Greek word is the same one used for household slaves, and the paradox here depends on it: the readers are free because they belong to God. The word for the slaves addressed in 2:18 is different (oiketai, 'household slaves'). Compare Jude 1:1, 'a slave of Jesus Christ', and Romans 6:22.

p: Adelphotes, 'brotherhood', means the whole family of believers.
b: The noun is found in the New Testament only here and in 5:9. It names the Christian community as a family. The verse sets four commands side by side: honor all people, love the brothers, fear God, honor the king. Only God is feared, while the king receives the honor due to all people. Proverbs 24:21 says 'Fear the LORD, my son, and fear the king'; Peter's line seems to change it on purpose.

p: Oiketai were slaves in a household: cooks, nurses, teachers, managers, laborers.
b: Peter uses oiketes, 'member of the household', not the general doulos. Slaves were a large part of the population of the cities of Asia Minor. Unlike the household codes of Ephesians 6:5-9 and Colossians 3:22-4:1, Peter says nothing to masters, perhaps because few of the readers were masters, or because the slaves he addresses had unbelieving owners. He speaks to slaves directly as members of the church, responsible before God.

t: Crooked masters, and how the verse was used
p: Skolios means bent or crooked; the KJV has 'froward'. Defenders of American slavery preached this teaching to slaves.
b: Peter tells slaves to submit even to harsh masters, a hard word that slaveholders later used. In A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin (1853, part 4, chapter 9) Harriet Beecher Stowe quotes sermons to slaves by Bishop William Meade of Virginia. One tells slaves that when they are punished, 'whether you really deserve it or not, it is your duty, and Almighty God requires, that you bear it patiently', and that 'the punishment you suffer unjustly here shall turn to your exceeding great glory hereafter', language close to 2:19-20. Stowe answers that such discourses 'appear hard-hearted and unfeeling to the last degree'. Peter's own grounds are different: God sees unjust suffering (2:19-20) and Christ suffered unjustly too (2:21-23). He does not call the master's harshness right; he calls the suffering unjust. On what the churches teach about slavery now, see the cards at Ephesians 6 and Philemon.

p: Charis here may mean 'what earns God's favor' or simply 'grace'.
b: In ordinary Greek charis could mean favor, thanks or credit. Luke 6:32-34 uses it this way: 'what thanks do you have coming?' Peter's 'This is grace' (2:19) and 'that is grace before God' (2:20) probably mean that unjust suffering borne for God's sake is what wins God's approval. The Plain keeps 'grace' because the letter uses the word so often for God's gift (1:2, 10, 13; 4:10; 5:10, 12), and the two meanings may be meant together.

p: Kolaphizo is to punch or slap, the word for the blows Jesus received.
b: The verb is used of the men who struck Jesus at his trial (Matthew 26:67; Mark 14:65). A slave's body was open to such treatment. Peter's next words, about Christ who suffered and did not strike back (2:21-23), tie the slave's experience to Jesus' own.

p: Hypogrammos was the line of letters a teacher wrote for a child to copy.
b: Children learning to write traced over or copied a teacher's model letters. Christ's suffering is the model; the readers are to copy it by tracing over it. 'His tracks' (ichnesin) are footprints, a second picture: walk where he walked. This is the only use of hypogrammos in the New Testament.

a: He did no sin, nor was trickery found in his mouth
p: The passage weaves together lines of Isaiah 53, the song of the suffering servant.
b: 2:22 quotes Isaiah 53:9 ('no deceit was in his mouth'); 2:24 draws on Isaiah 53:4-5, 12 ('He bore the sin of many', 'by his welts healing came to us'); 2:25 on Isaiah 53:6 ('We had all strayed like sheep'). The Greek of Isaiah 53:9 has 'he did no lawlessness'; Peter has 'sin'. This is one of the fullest uses of Isaiah 53 in the New Testament. Jewish interpreters have usually read the servant as Israel or a righteous figure in Israel; Christians since the New Testament have read it of Jesus. See the topic The Servant of the LORD.

t: Handing it over to the judge
p: The Greek does not say what Jesus handed over: himself, his cause, or his enemies.
b: Paredidou has no object. Many supply 'himself' (compare Luke 23:46, 'Father, into your hands I place my spirit'). Others supply 'his cause' or 'those who wronged him': he left judgment to God instead of threatening. The Plain says 'it all' to leave the choice open. The imperfect tense pictures an action kept up through the whole ordeal.
orig: παρεδίδου δὲ τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως (paredidou de to krinonti dikaios)

a: carried our sins up in his body onto the tree
p: Aneneken is also the word for offering a sacrifice up on an altar.
b: The verb anaphero can mean 'carry up' and is the usual Greek Old Testament word for offering a sacrifice up on the altar (Leviticus 14:20). Compare 2:5, 'bring spiritual sacrifices', the same verb. Isaiah 53:12 uses it in 'He bore the sin of many'. 'The tree' (xylon) is a word for the cross, recalling Deuteronomy 21:23 (compare Acts 5:30; Galatians 3:13). Readers have seen here Christ bearing the penalty of sins (substitution), Christ taking sins away, and Christ as the pattern for the readers to die to sin. See the topic Atonement.
orig: ἀνήνεγκεν ... ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον (anenenken ... epi to xylon)

a: By his welts you were healed
p: Molops is the welt left by a whip, the word of Isaiah 53:5.
b: Isaiah 53:5 reads 'by his welts healing came to us'. Peter turns it to 'you': the slaves he has just addressed, who might bear such welts themselves, are told that Christ's welts healed them. Some read the healing as forgiveness, others as including bodily healing (Matthew 8:17 applies Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus' healings).

a: the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls
p: Episkopos, 'overseer', is the word behind English 'bishop'; here it is a title of Christ.
b: The site's word for episkopos is 'overseer', with a capital here because it is a title of Christ. The word later became the title of church leaders ('bishop'), and in 5:2 the elders are told to be 'overseeing' the flock, with the verb from the same root. The shepherd image of God is old (Psalm 23:1; Ezekiel 34:11-16), and Jesus calls himself 'the good shepherd' (John 10:11). In 5:4 Christ is 'the Chief Shepherd'.
orig: τὸν ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον (ton poimena kai episkopon)

a: submit yourselves to your own husbands
t: A believing wife in an unbelieving house
p: Peter speaks to wives whose husbands did not share their faith: a dangerous position in a Roman home.
b: A respectable wife was expected to worship her husband's gods. Plutarch's Advice to Bride and Groom (section 19) says a wife should 'worship and know only the gods that her husband believes in' and 'shut the front door tight upon all queer rituals and outlandish superstitions' (the Loeb translation of F. C. Babbitt). A wife who joined the Christians broke that rule. Peter does not tell her to give up her faith; he tells her to keep it and to win her husband 'without a word' by the way she lives. Ephesians 5:22 ('Wives, to your own husbands, as to the Lord') and Colossians 3:18 use the same verb; on what 'submit' means for Christians today, see the card at Ephesians 5.

p: A play on words: husbands who will not obey 'the word' can be won 'without a word'.
b: Logos means first 'the word' (the message of the good news) and then 'a word' (talk). Peter does not forbid wives to speak of their faith; he says that where preaching is refused, a changed life can still persuade. 'Won over' (kerdaino) is the word Paul uses for winning people to Christ (1 Corinthians 9:19-22).

p: En phobo: in fear of God, or in respect toward the husband?
b: Peter uses 'fear' for the fear of God (1:17; 2:17), and he tells wives not to be frightened by any terror (3:6) and the readers not to fear what their opponents fear (3:14). So most readers take 'in fear' here as reverence for God. Others read it as respect toward the husband, as in Ephesians 5:33.

a: the braiding of hair, the putting on of gold
p: Elaborate hairstyles and jewelry marked wealth and status in Roman cities.
b: 1 Timothy 2:9 says much the same, and Isaiah 3:16-24 mocks the jewelry of Jerusalem's proud women. Peter does not forbid clothing (the Greek says 'the wearing of clothes', which no one could forbid); he contrasts outward adorning with the beauty of the heart.

p: Praus and hesychios: gentleness and quiet, virtues praised in men as well as women.
b: Praus is the word Jesus uses of himself, 'gentle and humble in heart' (Matthew 11:29), and of the meek who will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). Peter asks all believers to answer opponents 'gently' (3:15). Hesychios means calm and settled; 1 Timothy 2:2 prays for 'a calm and quiet life' for all. These are not qualities only for women, though Peter speaks of them here to wives.
orig: τοῦ πραέως καὶ ἡσυχίου πνεύματος (tou praeos kai hesychiou pneumatos)

p: Peter's example comes from Genesis 18:12, where Sarah laughs to herself.
b: The only place Sarah calls Abraham 'lord' is when she laughs inside herself at the promise of a son: 'After I am worn out, will I have pleasure, and my lord old too?' (Genesis 18:12). It is not a scene of obedience; Peter draws on her way of speaking about her husband. In Genesis it is also Abraham who listens to Sarah (Genesis 21:12). Peter's point for his readers is that wives who do good without fear are Sarah's daughters, as believers are Abraham's children (Galatians 3:7).

a: are not frightened by any terror
p: The phrase may echo Proverbs 3:25 in the Greek.
b: Ptoesis, 'terror', is rare in the Bible; the Greek of Proverbs 3:25 uses it: 'do not be afraid of sudden terror'. For a wife whose faith defied her husband's gods, fear of him or of what he might do was real. Peter tells her not to be ruled by it.
orig: μὴ φοβούμεναι μηδεμίαν πτόησιν (me phoboumenai medemian ptoesin)

p: Asthenesteron skeuos: 'weaker' in what sense is debated; 'vessel' means body or person.
b: Skeuos is a pot or a tool, and is used of the human body or person (1 Thessalonians 4:4; 2 Corinthians 4:7). 'Weaker' is a comparative: both are vessels. Readers have taken it as physical strength, as a woman's weaker legal and social position in a Roman household, or as moral or mental weakness, a reading many readers today reject. Peter draws the opposite of the usual conclusion: the weaker is to be given honor, and the wife is a co-heir of the same grace.

a: co-heirs with you of the grace of life
p: Husband and wife inherit the same life: the wife is not a junior partner in salvation.
b: Synkleronomos, 'co-heir', is the word for children who share an estate. Paul uses it of Gentiles who share Israel's inheritance (Ephesians 3:6) and of believers who share Christ's (Romans 8:17). Peter calls the wife her husband's equal heir of 'the grace of life'. If the husband ignores this, his prayers are 'cut off'. The manuscripts differ on whether the word describes the wives or the husbands: see the variant.

p: Peter echoes Jesus' teaching, as Paul does in Romans 12.
b: Jesus said 'Bless the ones who curse you. Pray for the ones who abuse you' (Luke 6:28), and Paul 'Bless your persecutors. Bless them, and never curse' and 'Pay no one back evil for evil' (Romans 12:14, 17). Peter's readers were being slandered (2:12; 3:16; 4:4). Christ himself 'gave no abuse back' (2:23). The goal, 'so that blessing would be your inheritance', recalls the blessing promised to Abraham (Genesis 12:2-3).

a: the one who wants to love life
p: 3:10-12 quotes Psalm 34:12-16 in a form close to its Greek.
b: The site's Psalm 34:12-16, from the Hebrew, reads 'Is there anyone who wants life, / who longs for days of seeing good?' and goes on 'Keep your tongue away from evil'. Peter turns the psalm's question into a statement and its commands into the third person ('must stop his tongue'). He leaves out the last line of 34:16, 'to wipe their memory from the earth', perhaps because he still hopes the readers' opponents will be won (2:12; 3:1). The psalm's title sets it in the time when David was driven out by a foreign king (Psalm 34:0).

p: Peter repeats the blessing of Jesus' Sermon on the Mount.
b: Jesus said 'Blessed are those who have suffered persecution on account of righteousness, because the kingdom of heaven is theirs' (Matthew 5:10), and the Plain follows its wording 'on account of righteousness'. Peter says it again in 4:14 ('If you are insulted over the name of Christ, you are blessed'), close to Matthew 5:11. 'If you do suffer' is a Greek form for something possible but not certain: not every believer was suffering at the moment.

a: Do not fear what they fear
p: Peter quotes Isaiah's word to the prophet's circle in a time of panic.
b: The site's Isaiah 8:12 reads 'What they fear, do not fear; / do not tremble before it', and 8:13 'It is the LORD of Armies you must count holy.' Peter's Greek, close to the Septuagint, can also mean 'Do not fear them', that is, do not be afraid of the threats of your opponents. In Isaiah the LORD is the one to be counted holy; Peter puts 'Christ' as 'Lord' in that place (3:15), as he did with the stone of Isaiah 8:14 (2:8).
orig: τὸν δὲ φόβον αὐτῶν μὴ φοβηθῆτε (ton de phobon auton me phobethete)

a: count Christ as Lord and holy
t: Christ in the place of the LORD
p: Isaiah 8:13 says to count the LORD holy; Peter writes 'Christ as Lord'.
b: The Greek of Isaiah 8:13 reads 'Count the Lord himself holy'. Peter writes kyrion de ton Christon hagiasate, 'count Christ holy as Lord' (or 'count the Lord, Christ, holy'). Here a text about Israel's God is applied to Jesus, as in 2:3 and 2:8. The Byzantine text and the KJV have 'the Lord God' instead: see the variant.

p: Apologia was a speech in reply to a charge, in court or in public.
b: The word is used of Paul's speeches before crowds and governors (Acts 22:1; 25:16; 2 Timothy 4:16). It is the source of 'apologetics', the reasoned defense of the faith. Here it is any answer, formal or informal, to 'anyone who asks you to account for the hope that is in you'. Peter adds how: 'gently and with fear', which in this letter means with fear of God, not of people (3:14).

p: Hapax: one time, and so never to be repeated.
b: Hebrews uses the same word and its strengthened form for Christ's sacrifice offered 'once' (Hebrews 9:26-28; 10:10), and Romans 6:10 says 'He died once for all'. The point here is that Christ's suffering is complete; the readers' sufferings are not added to it, but follow its pattern (4:1).

p: Prosago is the word for bringing someone into a king's presence, or an offering to the altar.
b: In the Greek Old Testament the verb is used of bringing priests and offerings near to God (Exodus 29:4; Leviticus 1:2). Its noun is the 'access' of Ephesians 2:18 and Romans 5:2. Christ suffered 'the one who was righteous for those who were not' so that people far from God could be brought into his presence.

a: in the spirit he was made alive
p: Many read flesh and spirit here as two spheres or ways of existing, not two parts of Christ.
b: Thanatotheis men sarki zoopoietheis de pneumati sets the two datives side by side. Many scholars read them as two realms: in the human, earthly realm he was put to death; in the realm of the Spirit, God's life, he was raised (compare Romans 1:3-4; 1 Timothy 3:16). The KJV has 'quickened by the Spirit', making the Holy Spirit the agent of the resurrection. Others read 'in his spirit', meaning Christ's human spirit lived on after death. The Plain says 'in the spirit', lowercase, which leaves the choice open; 4:6 uses the same contrast for believers.

a: made a proclamation to the spirits in prison
t: Who were the spirits, and what did he proclaim?
p: One of the hardest verses in the New Testament. Three main readings.
b: 1. Fallen angels. In Jewish writings the angels who sinned before the flood (Genesis 6:1-4) were held in a prison: 'This place is the prison of the angels' (1 Enoch 21:10), and in 1 Enoch 12-16 Enoch goes to announce their judgment. On this reading the risen Christ announced his victory over them (compare 3:22). Friedrich Spitta (1890) and Joachim Jeremias argued for it, and Stanley Porter credits Edward Selwyn (1946) with its wide influence today. 2. The dead of Noah's day. Christ, between his death and resurrection, went to the dead and preached, to announce salvation or judgment (Catholic and Orthodox teaching on the descent; Calvin took them as the souls of the godly dead). 3. Christ in Noah. Augustine (Letter 164) argued that Christ, in the spirit, preached through Noah to the people of his day, whose spirits are now in prison. Thomas Aquinas set out the descent reading and then judged that Augustine 'furnishes a better exposition': the preaching 'is not to be referred to Christ's descent into hell' (Summa Theologiae III, question 52, article 2). See the deep dive on this chapter and the card 'Where Christians differ'.
orig: τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασιν πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξεν (tois en phylake pneumasin poreutheis ekeryxen)
r: Genesis 6:1-4; 1 Enoch 21:10; 1 Enoch 12:4; 2 Peter 2:4-5; Jude 1:6; 4:6; Ephesians 4:9

a: In the spirit, too, he went
t: 'In which': in the spirit, or 'at that time'?
p: En ho most likely means 'in which' (the spirit), but may mean 'at which time' or 'for which reason'.
b: If en ho refers back to 'spirit' at the end of 3:18, Christ went 'in the spirit' (in his risen life, or in his spirit before the resurrection). Some take it as a joining phrase, 'and so' or 'on that occasion'. The Plain repeats 'In the spirit' so the reader can see the link most interpreters make. 'Went' (poreutheis) is the same word used of his going into heaven in 3:22, which some take as a sign that this journey too happened after the resurrection.
orig: ἐν ᾧ καὶ ... πορευθεὶς (en ho kai ... poreutheis)

p: Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives: eight people (Genesis 7:7, 13).
b: Genesis 7:13 names them: 'Noah went into the ark, with Shem, Ham and Japheth, Noah's sons, and Noah's wife, and his sons' three wives with them.' 2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah 'the eighth one'. Peter stresses that the saved were 'a few', a comfort to a small and slandered minority.

p: Di' hydatos may mean 'through the water' (they passed through it) or 'by water' (water was the means).
b: Dia with the genitive can be place ('through') or means ('by means of'). The flood water drowned the world but carried the ark; so water was both judgment and rescue. That double sense is what lets Peter move to baptism in the next verse. Isaiah 54:9 had already made 'the waters of Noah' a sign of God's promise.

p: In the Greek, 'baptism' is the subject of 'saves'. The small word that begins the verse can be read more than one way.
b: The Greek runs ho kai hymas antitypon nyn sozei baptisma, word for word 'which also you, as counterpart, now saves, baptism'. Baptisma is the subject of sozei, 'saves', and the Plain makes it so. The questions are about the rest. (1) Ho, 'which', is neuter, and the nearest neuter noun is 'water' (3:20): 'baptism, the counterpart of that water, saves you', the Plain's reading. (2) Some read ho as the subject, with 'baptism' added to name it: 'which, as a counterpart, now saves you too: baptism'. On this reading the water, in its counterpart, is in a sense what saves. (3) Antitypon can describe 'baptism' itself: 'the baptism that corresponds to it'. Scrivener's 1894 Textus Receptus prints a different form of the first word, ὧ, 'to which', the reading behind the KJV's 'The like figure whereunto'; Stephanus' 1550 edition and the critical editions have ὃ, 'which'. In every reading, 'not the removing of dirt from the flesh' and 'through the resurrection' say how baptism saves.
orig: ὃ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σῴζει βάπτισμα (ho kai hymas antitypon nyn sozei baptisma)

p: Antitypon is something that answers to a pattern, like a seal's impression to the seal.
b: Typos was the stamp or mold; antitypos the impression or copy that matches it. Peter says the water of the flood has its counterpart in the water of baptism. The word is one of the sources of 'antitype' in Christian 'typology', the reading of Old Testament events as patterns fulfilled later. Hebrews 9:24, its only other New Testament use, has it the other way around, for the earthly sanctuary as a copy of the true one in heaven ('a copy of the true one'). Calvin wrote that the apostle 'only means that there is a likeness'. The Plain says 'counterpart' to keep the matching-pair sense.

p: One of the plainest verses in the New Testament on baptism saving, and one of the most debated.
b: Peter says outright that baptism 'saves', and then at once says how: not as a bath, but as the pledge (or appeal) of a good conscience made to God, and 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ'. Churches that teach baptismal regeneration (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and the Anglican Prayer Book) read the verse as it stands: God saves through baptism. Churches that see baptism as a sign of a salvation already received (Baptists, many Reformed and evangelical Christians) stress the qualifications: what saves is not the water but what it signifies, and the power is Christ's resurrection. See the card 'Where Christians differ' on this chapter, and the cards at Mark 16:16, Acts 2:38 and Titus 3:5.
r: Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38; Romans 6:3-4; Colossians 2:12; Titus 3:5; Acts 22:16

a: the pledge of a good conscience made to God
p: Eperotema can be 'a request, appeal' or 'a pledge, a formal answer'.
b: The noun comes from a verb meaning 'ask'. In ordinary Greek it was 'a question' or 'a request', hence 'an appeal to God for a good conscience'. It can also mean the reply given to such a question, hence 'pledge', 'response' or 'answer' (the KJV has 'the answer of a good conscience'); the NET Bible notes all three as possible. The genitive 'of a good conscience' may be the source (a good conscience makes the pledge) or the thing asked for (an appeal for a clean conscience). Calvin took it as 'answer' or testimony.
orig: συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς θεόν (syneideseos agathes eperotema eis theon)

a: angels, authorities and powers have been placed under him
p: Christ at God's right hand, with the spiritual powers made subject, as Psalm 110:1 promised.
b: Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New Testament, says 'Sit at my right hand, / until I set your enemies down / as a stool for your feet.' Ephesians 1:20-21 places the risen Christ 'far above every ruler, authority, power and lordship', and Colossians 2:15 says he 'stripped the rulers and the authorities bare'. If the spirits of 3:19 are fallen angels, this verse completes the thought: his proclamation was of this victory. 'Placed under' uses the same verb as the readers' 'submit yourselves' (2:13, 18; 3:1).

p: Does suffering end sin, or is this about Christ, or about baptism?
b: The saying 'the one who has suffered in the flesh has broken with sin' is read several ways: of Christ, who by suffering finished with sin once for all; of the believer who has died with Christ in baptism (Romans 6:7, 'the one who has died has been set free from sin'); or as a general saying that people willing to suffer for their faith have made a clean break with a sinful life. It does not mean that suffering itself makes a person sinless.

p: The list describes the drinking parties and temple feasts of a Greek city.
b: Komoi were drunken revels that spilled into the streets; potoi drinking bouts. Romans 13:13 lists 'wild parties and drunkenness' too. Meals were often held in honor of the gods, some in temples (compare 1 Corinthians 8:10, 'sitting at a meal in an idol's temple'). 'Forbidden idol worship' (athemitois eidololatriais) is idol worship that God's law forbids. That Peter says his readers once lived this way is the main reason many think most of them were Gentiles (see the note at 1:1).

p: Blasphemountes may mean slandering the readers or blaspheming God.
b: The verb means speaking abuse, against people or against God. Here it probably means that the neighbors speak abuse of the believers who no longer join them, but some read it as abuse of God or Christ. Pliny, governor of Bithynia-Pontus around AD 112, wrote that those who denied being Christians proved it when they offered incense and wine to the emperor's image 'and moreover cursed Christ', and that temples 'which had been almost deserted' were being visited again.

a: to judge the living and the dead
t: Judge of the living and the dead
p: A phrase of early Christian preaching that entered the creeds.
b: Peter's speech to Cornelius says God has 'marked him out to judge the living and the dead' (Acts 10:42), and 2 Timothy 4:1 has the same phrase. The Apostles' Creed later said Christ 'will come to judge the living and the dead'. 'The one who is prepared to judge' may be God the Father (1:17) or Christ.

a: the good news was announced even to the dead
p: Which dead? Those Christ visited after his death, or believers who have died since?
b: Many read this with 3:19: Christ announced good news to the dead in Hades, so that they might live (the view of the Catholic Catechism, which cites this verse at 634, and of many Orthodox writers). Many modern scholars read it instead of Christians who heard the gospel while alive and have since died: their neighbors judged them in the flesh (and they died like everyone), but they will live 'in the spirit by God's measure'. A third view takes 'the dead' as the spiritually dead, people dead in sin. The Latter-day Saints read the verse as part of the basis for teaching the gospel to the dead in the spirit world.

a: The end of all things has come close
p: Engiken is Jesus' word: 'the kingdom of God has come near' (Mark 1:15).
b: Peter expects the end soon, as Paul, James and Revelation do (Romans 13:12; James 5:8; Revelation 22:10). Readers differ: some say the first Christians expected the end in their lifetime and were mistaken; some that 'near' describes the last age, which began with Christ (1:20) and could end at any time; some (preterists) apply it to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Peter draws practical conclusions: clear thinking, prayer, love, hospitality, gifts used for others.

a: love lays a cover over a great number of sins
p: Peter quotes Proverbs 10:12 in a form closer to the Hebrew than to the Septuagint.
b: The site's Proverbs 10:12 reads 'Hatred rouses fights, / but love lays a cover over all wrongdoing.' The Septuagint has something different ('friendship covers all who do not love strife'). Peter and James 5:20 have 'covers a great number of sins'. Readers take this as love that overlooks and forgives the sins of others in the church (the sense of Proverbs), or less often as love that wins forgiveness for one's own sins. The Plain uses the wording of Proverbs 10:12, 'lays a cover over'.

a: Open your homes to one another as guests
p: Christians traveling between cities depended on believers' homes.
b: Philoxenoi is literally 'loving strangers'. Traveling believers, messengers like Silvanus (5:12) and teachers needed homes to stay in. Churches met in homes too. 'Without grumbling' admits that this could be a burden. Romans 12:13, Hebrews 13:2 and 3 John 1:5-8 urge the same.

p: Oikonomos was the manager of a household, often a slave trusted with the master's goods.
b: Each believer has received a charisma, 'gift', and is to manage it as a steward manages what belongs to the owner. Jesus' parables use the same figure (Luke 12:42; 16:1-8), and Paul calls apostles 'stewards of the mysteries of God' (1 Corinthians 4:1). Peter divides the gifts into speaking and serving (4:11).

p: Logia theou: God's spoken words.
b: The phrase is used of the Scriptures entrusted to Israel (Romans 3:2, 'the oracles of God') and of God's words given to Moses (Acts 7:38). Whoever speaks in the church should speak as one handing on God's words, not his own opinions. 'To him belong the glory and the might' may refer to God or to Jesus Christ, the nearest name.

p: Pyrosis is a burning, the refiner's fire of 1:7.
b: The noun is used in the Greek of Proverbs 27:21 for the furnace that tests silver and gold. It recalls 1:7 ('fire tests it'). Some take it as a sign that a fierce new persecution had begun, others as the letter's picture for all the sufferings already described. Revelation 18:9 uses the noun for Babylon's burning.

p: Koinoneite: the readers are partners in Christ's sufferings.
b: Paul speaks of 'sharing in his sufferings' (Philippians 3:10) and of making up what is lacking in them (Colossians 1:24). Peter does not say that their suffering adds to Christ's work, which was 'a single time' (3:18); rather, those who suffer as Christians stand where he stood and will share his glory (5:1).
orig: κοινωνεῖτε τοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθήμασιν (koinoneite tois tou Christou pathemasin)

a: the Spirit of glory, the Spirit of God, comes to rest on you
p: The words echo Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit rests on the coming king.
b: The site's Isaiah 11:2 reads 'The LORD's Spirit will come to rest on him', and its Greek uses the same verb as Peter, anapauomai. What Isaiah said of the shoot from Jesse's stump is said here of insulted believers. Jesus promised that the Spirit would speak through the disciples when they were brought before authorities (Matthew 10:19-20). 'The Spirit of glory' may also recall God's glory resting on the tabernacle.
orig: τὸ τῆς δόξης καὶ τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεῦμα (to tes doxes kai to tou theou pneuma)

a: a busybody in other people's affairs
p: Allotriepiskopos is found only here in the Bible.
b: The word joins allotrios, 'belonging to someone else', and episkopos, 'overseer'. It may mean a meddler, someone who interferes in others' business; an informer; someone who embezzles goods placed in their care; or a Christian who stirs trouble by interfering in pagan customs. Since it stands next to murderer and thief, some think it names a crime. The Plain gives the most common reading.

p: One of only three uses of the word in the New Testament, and the one tied to suffering.
b: Acts 11:26 says 'Antioch was the first place where the disciples came to be called "Christians"', and King Agrippa uses the word in Acts 26:28. The ending -ianos is Latin, used for followers of a person or party. Around AD 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia-Pontus (one of the regions this letter addresses), asked the emperor Trajan whether 'the name itself, even without offenses', should be punished; Trajan replied that Christians 'are not to be sought out', but those accused and proved were to be punished. Some scholars date 1 Peter to that time; others note that hostility to the name was older (Nero's punishment of Christians in Rome in AD 64).

a: judgment to start from God's house
p: The prophets spoke of God's judgment starting with his own people and temple.
b: In Ezekiel's vision God says 'Start at my sanctuary' (Ezekiel 9:6), and in Jeremiah 25:29 'Look, I am beginning to bring harm on the city that is called by my name.' Malachi 3:1-5 pictures the Lord coming to his temple to purify the priests. Peter has called the believers God's 'spiritual house' (2:5), and now says that the testing they suffer is the start of God's judgment, which will fall harder on those who refuse the good news.

a: if the righteous person is barely saved
p: Peter quotes the Septuagint of Proverbs 11:31, which differs from the Hebrew.
b: The site's Proverbs 11:31, from the Hebrew, reads 'Look: if the righteous get their due here on earth, / how much more the wicked man and the sinner!' The Greek translators read the verse differently: 'If the righteous is barely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?' Peter quotes the Greek word for word. Both forms make the same argument from the lesser to the greater; the Greek makes it about salvation through hardship.

a: entrust their souls to the Creator, who is faithful
p: Paratithemi is the word Jesus used on the cross in Luke 23:46.
b: Jesus cried 'Father, into your hands I place my spirit' (Luke 23:46), quoting Psalm 31:5. Peter uses the same verb for believers who suffer: they place their lives with God as a deposit with a trustworthy keeper, while they go on doing good. This is the only place in the New Testament where God is called 'Creator' (ktistes): the one who made them can be trusted to keep them.

p: The apostle speaks to the elders as one of them: what that says about church office is debated.
b: Sympresbyteros occurs only here. Peter does not command as an apostle but appeals as an elder among elders. Catholic readers note that he still exhorts the elders of five regions, which fits his place among the apostles (see the cards at Matthew 16:18 and John 21:15-17 on Peter and the papacy). Many Protestant readers see here a model of shared leadership and point out that Peter claims no rank above other elders. Critical scholars who think a later writer used Peter's name read the title as a way of giving the letter his authority while addressing church leaders of the writer's own time.

a: a witness of the sufferings of Christ
p: Martys is one who saw, and one who testifies.
b: Peter was present at Jesus' arrest and trial, and denied him (Mark 14:54, 66-72); the Gospels do not place him at the cross. 'Witness' may mean an eyewitness of the events of Christ's passion, or one who testifies to them, as all the apostles did (Acts 1:8; 2:32). Later the word came to mean a 'martyr', one whose death is a witness, and early Christian writers (1 Clement 5) say Peter died as one.

p: Peter passes on to the elders the charge Jesus gave him.
b: In John 21:16 Jesus tells Peter 'Shepherd my sheep', with the same verb poimaino. Paul gives the elders of Ephesus the same charge (Acts 20:28: 'to shepherd the church of God'). The flock is God's, not the elders'. 'Overseeing' (episkopountes) shares its root with episkopos, 'overseer', the word later used for bishops; in this verse elders oversee, as in Acts 20:17, 28 and Titus 1:5-7.

a: not out of greed for dirty money
p: Aischrokerdos, 'for shameful gain', implies that elders could be paid or handled church funds.
b: Related words are used of church leaders elsewhere: the adjective 'greedy for dirty money' of deacons and overseers (1 Timothy 3:8; Titus 1:7), and the phrase 'dirty gain' in Titus 1:11. Peter uses the adverb. Elders may have received support (1 Timothy 5:17-18) or managed money for the poor. The danger was serving for what one could get.

p: The verb is the one Jesus used of the rulers of the nations.
b: Jesus told the Twelve that among the nations 'those who are thought of as their rulers act as lords over them', and 'That is not how it is with you' (Mark 10:42-43). Peter, who heard those words, uses the same verb, katakyrieuo. 'Those allotted to you' (ton kleron, 'the shares') are the congregations assigned to each elder's care; the word kleros is the source of English 'clergy', though here it means the people, not the leaders.

a: the wreath of glory that never withers
p: Stephanos was a wreath of leaves given to winners at the games; real wreaths withered fast.
b: Winners at the games received wreaths of leaves, which soon dried. Peter promises one that 'never withers' (amarantinos, related to the 'cannot wither' of 1:4). Paul uses the same contrast in 1 Corinthians 9:25. James 1:12 and Revelation 2:10 speak of 'the crown of life'.
orig: τὸν ἀμαράντινον τῆς δόξης στέφανον (ton amarantinon tes doxes stephanon)

p: Here presbyteroi may mean the church's elders or simply older people.
b: In 5:1-4 'elders' are church leaders. Here they are set against 'younger ones' (neoteroi), so some take the word in its everyday sense, 'older people'. In the first churches leaders were usually chosen from among the older men, so both senses may be present.

p: Enkombooomai is to tie something on with a knot, like a work apron.
b: The verb comes from kombos, a knot. Some see a picture of the apron slaves tied on to serve; many readers have recalled Jesus tying a towel around himself to wash the disciples' feet (John 13:4-5), a scene in which Peter had a part (John 13:6-9). The quotation that follows is Proverbs 3:34 in the Greek.

a: God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace
p: Peter, like James 4:6, quotes the Septuagint of Proverbs 3:34.
b: The site's Proverbs 3:34, from the Hebrew, reads 'Mockers he mocks, / but the humble he gives his favor.' The Greek, which Peter and James quote, has 'the Lord sets himself against the proud, but gives grace to the humble'; both letters put 'God' for 'the Lord'. James 4:6 on this site reads 'God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace', and the Plain here is the same.

p: 'A strong hand' is the Exodus phrase for God's rescue of Israel from Egypt.
b: Deuteronomy says the LORD 'brought you out with a strong hand and ransomed you from the house of slaves' (Deuteronomy 7:8; compare Deuteronomy 26:8). The hand that humbles is the hand that rescues. 'Lift you high at the right time' echoes Jesus' saying that 'whoever humbles himself will be lifted high' (Matthew 23:12; Luke 14:11).

a: Throw every worry you have onto him
p: Peter borrows the psalm's verb and its word for worry.
b: The site's Psalm 55:22 reads 'Throw your load on the LORD, / and he will provide for you'. The Greek of the psalm has 'Throw your worry (merimna) on the Lord', and Peter uses its verb and noun. Jesus' teaching 'do not worry' (Matthew 6:25-34) uses the same word family.
orig: πᾶσαν τὴν μέριμναν ὑμῶν ἐπιρίψαντες (pasan ten merimnan hymon epiripsantes)

p: Antidikos is an opponent in a lawsuit, the role of the accuser in Job and Zechariah.
b: Antidikos was the other party in a court case (Matthew 5:25). Diabolos, 'devil', means 'slanderer'. Both fit the accuser of Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1, and the readers' own experience of slander (2:12; 3:16). The roaring lion recalls Psalm 22:13 ('a lion ripping prey and roaring').
orig: ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν διάβολος (ho antidikos hymon diabolos)

p: James 4:7 gives the same command with the same verb.
b: James 4:7 on this site reads 'Stand up against the devil, and he will run away from you.' Both letters join humility before God (5:6; James 4:10) with resisting the devil, and both quote Proverbs 3:34 just before. Many scholars think both drew on common early Christian teaching. Ephesians 6:11-13 uses the same verb for standing in God's armor.

p: The readers are told that Christians across the world face the same pressure.
b: This line has been used in the debate about the letter's date. Some take it as evidence of a widespread persecution. John H. Elliott reads it the other way: the same kind of suffering everywhere points to scattered local hostility, not to official Roman persecution, since the first empire-wide persecution ordered by Rome came under Decius in AD 250. That fits the slander and insults the rest of the letter describes.

p: Four verbs pile up the promise: mend, make firm, strengthen, ground.
b: Katartizo is to mend or put in order (used of mending nets, Mark 1:19); sterizo to make firm (Jesus told Peter 'strengthen your brothers', with this verb, Luke 22:32); sthenoo to give strength; themelioo to lay a foundation. Some manuscripts lack the last verb: see the variant. The God who called them 'into his glory that lasts forever' will finish what he began.
orig: καταρτίσει, στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιώσει (katartisei, sterixei, sthenosei, themeliosei)

p: Dia Silouanou ... egrapsa: Silvanus may have drafted the letter, written it down, or carried it.
b: Silvanus is very likely the Silas of Acts, Paul's companion (Acts 15:22, 40), named 'Silvanus' in 1 Thessalonians 1:1 and 2 Corinthians 1:19. Egrapsa, 'I wrote', is the letter-writer's past tense, seen from the readers' side, so English says 'I have written'. 'Through' someone can name either of two roles. (1) Secretary or drafter. The 'secretarial hypothesis' holds that Peter dictated or approved the letter and Silvanus gave it its Greek form, which would explain its polished Greek. (2) Letter-carrier. 'Through' can name the one who brought a letter: the Jerusalem letter of Acts 15:23 is sent, in Greek, 'through their hand'. John H. Elliott argues that the wording names Silvanus as the courier, not the secretary. The Plain keeps 'through Silvanus' so both readings stay open. See the opening pages (Authorship).

t: Who is 'she', and where is Babylon?
p: 'She' is almost surely a church; 'Babylon' is most often read as Rome.
b: He en Babyloni syneklekte is feminine: 'the one in Babylon, chosen together with you'. A few have taken it as Peter's wife (1 Corinthians 9:5), but most read it as the church, since ekklesia is feminine and 'chosen' matches 1:1. As for Babylon: (1) Rome, the common view; Eusebius reports that Clement of Alexandria and Papias said Peter wrote 'in Rome itself' and called the city 'by a figure, Babylon'. Revelation calls the great city Babylon (Revelation 14:8; 17-18). (2) The city in Mesopotamia, held by Erasmus and Calvin, though there is no evidence Peter worked there. (3) A Roman fortress called Babylon in Egypt, near modern Cairo, mentioned by Strabo. Two late manuscripts add 'in Rome'.
orig: ἡ ἐν Βαβυλῶνι συνεκλεκτὴ (he en Babyloni syneklekte)

p: Very likely John Mark of Acts, whom early tradition links with Peter and with the Gospel of Mark.
b: Acts mentions 'Mary, mother of the John they called Mark', in whose house the church prayed when Peter was in prison (Acts 12:12). Mark traveled with Paul and Barnabas, left them, and was later with Paul again (Acts 15:37-39; Philemon 1:24; 2 Timothy 4:11, 'Pick up Mark and bring him along'). 'My son' is a term of affection for a disciple. Eusebius reports Papias' and Clement's account that Mark wrote down Peter's preaching in Rome, and that Peter 'makes mention of Mark in his first epistle'. See the topic Gospel of Mark.

p: Paul calls it 'a holy kiss'; Peter 'a kiss of love'.
b: The greeting kiss between family members became a sign of the church as a family (Romans 16:16, 'Greet one another with a holy kiss'; 1 Thessalonians 5:26). It later became part of the Eucharist liturgy in many churches, as 'the kiss of peace', and is still exchanged, in one form or another, in many traditions.

a: Peace to you, all who are in Christ
p: The letter ends as Jewish letters often did, with peace, and as it began (1:2).
b: The letter began with 'Grace to you, and peace' (1:2) and ends with peace. Paul's letters usually end with grace. 'In Christ' is a phrase Peter shares with Paul (3:16; 5:10). The Byzantine text adds 'Jesus. Amen': see the variant.
